Project Overview

For my MAE 214 final project, I modeled a shock absorber assembly in SolidWorks and prepared a drawing package connecting individual part geometry to the complete assembly. The work combines seven custom component designs with standard fastening hardware.

My Contribution

  • Modeled the bracket, spacer, shaft, U-support, bushing, pivot, and spring as individual components.
  • Integrated the components and fastening hardware into the assembled model shown in the final submission.
  • Created an exploded view with numbered callouts and a bill of materials listing part names, materials, and quantities.
  • Prepared seven component sheets with orthographic views, isometric views, dimensions, and thread or coil details where applicable.

Design Brief & Constraints

The assignment used a fictional design-engineer scenario for a Mercedes-Benz C-Class shock absorber. Reference figures supplied the starting geometry; the brief required students to revise dimensions where needed, account for missing parts, and communicate the assembly through engineering drawings.

These constraints come from the assignment brief and define the design task. They are separate from the results documented in my drawing package.

Fit and motion

Use the reference figures and supplied motion video to assemble the mechanism, adjusting geometry where necessary for the intended motion.

Interference limits

The brief permits up to 0.02 in³ of interference for threaded components. All other components must have no interference.

Drawing coverage

Provide dimensioned third-angle drawings for custom parts, plus an exploded assembly drawing and a bill of materials. The spring must be modeled by the student.

Materials and hardware

Choose suitable materials, including bronze bushings. Downloaded fasteners are permitted, with a separate appendix requested for their part numbers, descriptions, and materials.

Assembly Architecture & Bill of Materials

The exploded drawing makes the component relationships explicit: the pivot sits between a pair of bronze bushings in the U-support, while the shaft, spring, spacer, bracket, washer, and self-locking nut form the lower stack. A hex-head bolt, castle nut, and cotter pin complete the upper connection.

The spring's 1.845 helix-height note and 2.005 overall-height dimension are both retained from the sheet. They should not be reported as the same free-height measurement. The drawing documents geometry; it does not establish a spring rate or damping coefficient.

Materials & Manufacturing Considerations

Material Selection

Steel structure and hardware. The bill of materials specifies steel for the bracket, spacer, shaft, U-support, pivot, spring, and all five hardware types. It does not identify steel grades, heat treatments, or coatings.

Bronze bearing interfaces. Both bushings are listed as bronze. Their flanged geometry locates them at the pivot connection in the exploded assembly; the submission does not specify a bronze alloy or lubrication requirement.

From CAD to Fabrication

The drawings communicate different fabrication needs: rotational geometry for the shaft, spacer, and bushings; formed profiles and hole locations for the bracket and U-support; and coil geometry for the spring.

A manufacturing release would still need material grades, general and fit tolerances, surface-finish requirements, and confirmed hardware catalog references. These are next steps beyond the submitted CAD drawing package.

Outcomes & Next Steps

A traceable assembly package

The final submission contains an assembled model image, an exploded assembly/BOM sheet, and seven individually dimensioned component sheets. The numbered callouts connect every BOM item to its position in the assembly.

Component-to-assembly communication

Orthographic views capture dimensions and hole locations, while isometric views explain the shape of the formed supports, pivot, bushings, and spring. The shaft and spring sheets add their specific thread and coil callouts.

This is a CAD modeling and documentation project. The supplied PDFs do not include a motion study, interference-detection results, load analysis, or physical testing, so vehicle fit, suspension performance, and compliance with the interference limits remain unverified here.

Further Engineering Work

  • Record an interference check against the brief's limits and demonstrate the intended assembly motion with the correct degrees of freedom.
  • Add catalog part numbers and dimensions for the five hardware types in the requested fastener appendix.
  • Resolve manufacturing fits and tolerances, then analyze spring stiffness, operating loads, and travel before any prototype testing.
